description: Use financial, marketing and market data to support business decisions, and understand data limitations.
content_html:
Why Businesses Use Data

Every growing business generates and receives large amounts of data. Sales figures, customer feedback scores, market research surveys, competitor price lists — all of this can inform better decisions. The challenge is knowing which data to trust, how to read it accurately, and what it cannot tell you.

Business data falls into two broad categories. Quantitative data uses numbers — sales volumes, profit margins, market share percentages. Qualitative data captures opinions, descriptions and feelings — customer reviews, focus group transcripts, staff feedback. Both types have value; relying solely on one risks missing important information.

Types of Business Data

The specification identifies four main categories of data a business uses to understand performance and inform decisions:

  • Financial data — profit and loss figures, cash flow statements, balance sheet extracts, break-even analysis. Used to assess profitability, liquidity and financial health.
  • Marketing data — customer satisfaction scores, conversion rates, advertising response rates, social media engagement metrics. Used to assess how well marketing is reaching and influencing customers.
  • Market data — total market size, sales trends, competitor market share, growth rates. Used to assess a business’s position within its industry and spot opportunities or threats.
  • Data from graphs and charts — bar charts, line graphs, pie charts and scatter diagrams present numerical data visually, making trends and comparisons easier to identify quickly.
Key Fact

Market share is one of the most important market data measures. It shows not just how well a business is performing in absolute terms, but how it is performing relative to competitors. A business can increase its revenue while its market share falls — meaning rivals are growing faster.

Reading Graphs and Charts

When interpreting a graph or chart in an exam question, a systematic approach prevents simple errors:

  • Read the title and axis labels carefully before drawing any conclusions.
  • Check the units on each axis (thousands, millions, percentages, indices).
  • Identify the trend (rising, falling, stable, fluctuating) before stating specific values.
  • Note any anomalies — sudden spikes or dips — and consider what business event might explain them.

Market share is calculated as: (Business’s sales ÷ Total market sales) × 100

Example: Inkwell Stationers has annual sales of £2.4 million. The total UK stationery market is worth £30 million. Market share = (£2.4m ÷ £30m) × 100 = 8.00%.

A rising market share means the business is growing faster than its market. A falling market share is a warning signal even if total sales are rising — competitors are gaining ground. This distinction is important when using market data to justify business decisions.

Using Data to Support Decisions

Data is most valuable when it informs specific decisions. A falling net profit margin might prompt a business to review supplier costs. A declining market share may lead to a marketing campaign or product development. An improving customer satisfaction score may justify a price increase.

However, data should be used to support decisions rather than to make them automatically. Good business judgement combines data with context, experience and knowledge of the specific business’s circumstances. Two businesses can look at the same market data and make completely different, equally rational decisions based on their different strategies, resources and risk appetites.

Key Fact

Financial data is historical — it shows what has happened, not what will happen. A business with strong past profits can still fail if market conditions change rapidly. This is one reason why data must always be interpreted in the context of the wider business environment.

Limitations of Business Data

Understanding what data cannot tell you is just as important as knowing how to read it. Key limitations include:

  • Historical data is backward-looking. Financial statements show last year’s performance. A business making decisions based only on past data may miss new market trends or emerging threats.
  • Data can be misleading without context. A 10% rise in sales revenue looks positive, but not if it cost 25% more to achieve. Raw figures without comparison or context lead to poor decisions.
  • Quantitative data misses qualitative insight. A sales report cannot tell you why customers are buying less, or what they really think about the product. Qualitative research is needed to fill this gap.
  • Data accuracy depends on how it was collected. Sample sizes, survey bias, accounting policies and data recording errors all affect reliability. Decisions based on flawed data can be worse than decisions made with no data at all.
  • Market data may not reflect the specific business’s segment. National market size figures may not accurately represent the niche or region the business operates in.

Students often assume that a business with more data will make better decisions. In practice, too much data without the ability to filter, interpret and apply it can lead to “analysis paralysis” — delayed decisions while more information is gathered. The quality, relevance and timeliness of data matter more than the quantity. A small business that acts quickly on one reliable signal may outperform a large business drowning in dashboards it cannot interpret. In extended responses, always question whether the data available is sufficient and appropriate for the decision being made.
exam_tip_html: For “Identify from Data” (1 mark), read from the graph or table directly and state only what you are asked. Do not interpret or add context — a single accurate reading is all that is required. For “Evaluate a Statement” (12 marks) about data, your conclusion must introduce new evaluative thinking: identify the specific factor (data type, business context, reliability of the source) that determines whether the statement holds. Writing “it depends” earns nothing — but “it depends on whether the data is current, because historical financial figures cannot capture a sudden shift in consumer behaviour” earns evaluation marks. Make your criteria explicit.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Business data comes in four main types: financial, marketing, market and graphical. Quantitative data uses numbers; qualitative data captures opinions — both are needed for well-rounded decisions.
  • Market share = (business sales ÷ total market sales) × 100. A rising market share shows the business is outgrowing its market; a falling share is a warning signal even when total sales are rising.
  • Data has real limitations: it is historical, can mislead without context, and quantitative data cannot explain the 'why' behind trends. Strong business analysis acknowledges what the data cannot tell you.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows sales data for two businesses in the same market.

| Business | Annual sales |
|---|---|
| Apex Sportswear | £4,500,000 |
| Rival companies (combined) | £40,500,000 |

Identify the market share of Apex Sportswear.
A business had sales revenue of £80,000 in Year 1 and £100,000 in Year 2. The total market size was £500,000 in both years. Calculate the change in market share between Year 1 and Year 2.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks for the correct change in market share of +4 percentage points (from 16% to 20%).
1 mark for correctly calculating either Year 1 market share (16%) or Year 2 market share (20%) but not both.

Year 1: (£80,000 ÷ £500,000) × 100 = 16.00%
Year 2: (£100,000 ÷ £500,000) × 100 = 20.00%
Change = 20% − 16% = +4 percentage points.

practice_questions.text: Outline two limitations of using financial data when making business decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks. 1 mark for each limitation identified (up to 2), with 1 additional mark for developing one of them in context.

Acceptable limitations: financial data is backward-looking (shows past performance, not future); does not capture qualitative factors such as customer sentiment; figures can be affected by accounting policies, making comparisons unreliable; data from a single period may not reflect seasonal patterns or one-off events.

Development example: financial statements show last year's profit but cannot reveal whether a new competitor has entered the market since then, making future profit forecasts unreliable.

practice_questions.text: Analyse why a business that sees rising sales revenue might still be in a weakening competitive position.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks per analytical point (1 for a statement, 1 for development, 1 for further development or contextualisation).

Acceptable points:
- Rising revenue can mask a falling market share. If the total market is growing faster than the business, competitors are capturing most of the new customers — the business is growing, but losing ground relatively.
- Rising revenue does not guarantee rising profit. If costs have risen faster than revenue (e.g. higher supplier prices, wage increases), net profit margin will fall even as headline sales grow.
- Revenue growth can be achieved by cutting prices, which increases volume but reduces margins. The business looks busier but is less financially healthy per sale.

Mark the best two analytical chains.

practice_questions.text: Brindle & Co. is a small clothing brand in Sheffield. The owner has just received the following data: (1) annual sales have grown by 15% this year; (2) customer satisfaction scores have fallen from 82% to 71%; (3) the UK clothing market has grown by 22% in the same period. Discuss whether Brindle & Co. is in a strong business position based on this data.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Uses all three data points to build a nuanced argument. Recognises that 15% revenue growth sounds positive but that a 22% market growth rate means market share has fallen. Connects falling satisfaction scores to a future risk for revenue. Brings in the limitation that the data is quantitative and backward-looking. Reaches a substantiated view with evaluative criteria (e.g. the short-term revenue looks healthy but the structural signals are concerning).

Secure (5–7 marks): Uses at least two data points with analytical development. Acknowledges the apparent conflict between positive revenue growth and the two warning signals. Some evaluative thinking.

Developing (3–4 marks): Describes the data points with limited analysis. May note that satisfaction has fallen without developing what this means for future sales.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple observations about the data with no development.

practice_questions.text: 'Quantitative financial data is always the most useful type of data for making business decisions.' Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Develops a sophisticated argument that quantitative financial data is valuable for measuring performance and comparing over time, but has specific, well-explained limitations. Argues that qualitative data (customer insight, brand perception, employee motivation) can be equally important for strategic decisions that quantitative data cannot capture. Conclusion introduces a new evaluative criterion — such as the type of decision being made (operational vs strategic), the business's size or stage, or the reliability and recency of the data — rather than re-summarising. Shows awareness that the claim 'always' in the statement is its main weakness.

Secure (7–9 marks): Argues both sides with some development. Uses examples. Conclusion is present but may partly echo earlier points.

Developing (4–6 marks): Identifies strengths and weaknesses of financial data but analysis is general. May not address the 'always' qualifier.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points about data types with little analysis or structure.

knowledge_checks.q: A business has sales of £6 million. The total market is worth £40 million. What is the business's market share?
Which of the following is an example of qualitative data?
options: A business's net profit margin of 18%
Customer reviews describing the product as 'excellent quality'
A 12% rise in year-on-year sales revenue

knowledge_checks.q: Data expressed as numbers that can be measured and compared is called _____ data.
A key limitation of financial data is that it is _____, meaning it shows past performance rather than future prospects.
Match each data type to its correct example:
right: Profit and loss account showing gross profit of £90,000
Total UK soft drinks market worth £15 billion

flashcard_questions.a: Data expressed as numbers that can be measured and compared.
Data based on opinions, feelings or descriptions that cannot easily be measured in numbers.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a falling market share indicate, even when total sales are rising?
flashcard_questions.a: Competitors are growing faster and gaining ground in the market.
Data about the total market, including market size, trends, competitor shares and growth rates.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one limitation of using historical financial data for business decisions.
flashcard_questions.a: It shows past performance only and cannot capture recent market changes or future trends.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might rising revenue not mean a business is in a strong position?
flashcard_questions.a: If costs rise faster than revenue, profit margins fall even as sales grow.
How well marketing activities are reaching and influencing customers (e.g. conversion rates, satisfaction scores).

flashcard_questions.q: Why is qualitative data valuable alongside financial data?
flashcard_questions.a: It explains why customers behave as they do, which numbers alone cannot reveal.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the risk of basing business decisions entirely on quantitative data?
flashcard_questions.a: It misses qualitative insight into customer motivation and ignores factors that cannot be measured.

flashcard_questions.q: What should you check first when reading a business graph or chart?
flashcard_questions.a: The title and axis labels, including units, before drawing any conclusions.

glossary_terms.definition: Data expressed as numbers that can be measured and compared.
Data based on opinions, feelings or descriptions that cannot be easily measured in numbers.
A business's sales as a percentage of total sales in the market.
Numerical information about a business's money, including profit and loss figures, cash flow and break-even analysis.
Information used to assess how well marketing activities are reaching and influencing customers, such as satisfaction scores and conversion rates.
Information about the total market, including its size, growth rate, and competitors' shares, used to assess a business's position.
The degree to which data can be trusted to be accurate and appropriate for the decision being made; affected by sample size, bias and how data was collected.

items.title: More or Less: Behind the Statistics — BBC Radio 4
items.description: Tim Harford's BBC Radio 4 programme unpicks statistics used in news and business — perfect for understanding data limitations, misleading figures and how to read data critically.

items.title: Marketplace — Making Sense of Business Numbers
items.description: American Public Media's daily business programme explains market data, economic indicators and how companies interpret figures to make strategic decisions.

items.title: How Statistics Can Be Misleading — TED-Ed
items.description: Mark Liddell's animated TED-Ed lesson explains how the same data can support opposite conclusions — directly addresses the limitations of business data covered in this lesson.

items.title: The Beauty of Data Visualization — David McCandless
items.description: TED-Ed talk on how well-designed charts communicate complex business data clearly — and how poorly designed visuals mislead. Essential context for reading graphs under exam conditions.

items.title: Hans Rosling's 200 Countries, 200 Years — BBC
items.description: Hans Rosling brings statistical data to life with dynamic charts, demonstrating how trends, outliers and context transform raw numbers into powerful insights.

items.title: Moneyball (2011)
items.description: A real-world case study in using market data to challenge conventional wisdom — Billy Beane's team shows how analysing the right data beats relying on tradition and gut feeling.

items.title: Inside Job (2010)
items.description: Oscar-winning documentary on how businesses and regulators ignored warning data before the 2008 financial crisis — a vivid lesson in the consequences of data misinterpretation.

items.title: BBC Bitesize — Using Business Data to Make Decisions
items.description: Covers quantitative vs qualitative data, types of business data and how to read graphs and tables — matched to the Edexcel specification for this topic.

items.title: tutor2u — Interpreting Business Data
items.description: Exam-focused notes on market share calculations, reading charts, data limitations and how to structure analysis answers for 6- and 9-mark questions.

items.title: Office for National Statistics — Business and Economy Data
items.description: The ONS publishes real UK market size data, sector growth figures and business statistics — valuable for understanding what real market data looks like and how it is presented.
